This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to $n=p+2^k$ for prime $p$ and $k\geq 0$. Is it true that $f(n)=o(\log n)$?
#236: [Er55c][Er61][Er77c]
number theory | 
primes
Erdős [Er50] proved that there are infinitely many $n$ such that $f(n)\gg \log\log n$.
Erdős could not even prove that there do not exist infinitely many integers $n$ such that for all $1< 2^k<n$ the number $n-2^k$ is prime - see [1142].
The sequence of values of $f(n)$ is A109925 on the OEIS.
See also [237].
Additional thanks to: Alfaiz and Ralf Stephan

 Hooley in this paper has proved under the assumption of the extended Riemann Hypothesis, that integers $n$ such that for all $1<2^k<n$ the number $n-2^k$ is prime < $O(x^{1-\lambda+\epsilon})$ for any sufficiently small positive number $\epsilon$, where $\lambda = \Pi_p (1- \frac{1}{p(p-1)})$.
This was further improved by Narkiewicz in this paper to $O(x^{1-\lambda/\log2 +\epsilon})$ under the same assumption.
P.S. Improving on the result of Mientka and Weitzenkamp, Uchiyama and Yorinaga have proved there are no other such $n\leq 2^{77}$ in a two paper series - [1] and [2].

 Let $E_2(N)$ denote the number of natural numbers $n \leq N$ for which $n - 2^k$ is a prime number for all $k$ with $1 \leq k \leq \log_2 n$. Vaughan, in this paper, has showed that for some suitable positive number $c$ and for every sufficiently large $N$,\[E_2(N) < N \exp (- \frac{c \log N \log \log \log N}{\log \log N})\]Furthermore, Mientka and Weitzenkamp in this paper has verified that $7, 15, 21, 45, 75,$ and $105$ are the only values of $n$ for which $n - 2^k$ is a prime number for all $k$ with $1 \leq k \leq \log_2 n$ for $n \leq 2^{44}$.

 Why it suggests it barely?
If $2^k<n<2^{k+1}$, then except for $n-2^k$, all values to check are of the form $n-2^i>2^{k-1}$.
Hence the number of primes of the form $n-2^i$ is on average bounded by $3.$
Of course, there is some positive correlation on the chance, due to e.g. even vs odd, but so wondering which more detailed heuristical thoughts you had.

 For each $n$ in this range, there are $k$ values to check, each of which has about a $1/k$ chance of being prime, so the chance that they are all prime is about $1/k^k$... which dominates the total number of $n$ in this range, which is $2^k$ or so, but not by a huge margin... $\exp(-k \log k)$ versus $\exp(k)$.

 Ok, the terms barely and huge margin are here maybe subjective.
This reasoning could apply to the "Erdos could not even prove..." part as well.
Since $\exp(k) \exp(-k \log k) = \exp(- \Theta(k \log k))$, the chance of having really large counterexamples is very small.
But starting from $n>10^4$, it is indeed still a chance, and a formal proof for excluding that is far from obvious.
One deduces similar formulas for the probability (e.g. using Poisson approximation) that it is above $c \log k$, and since we are speaking about the limit, that should be the case.

 I guess for me "barely" is with regards to how optimal the bounds need to be in order to conclude the result. For instance if the heuristic prediction for density was $\exp(-k \log k)$ and one managed somehow to get an argument that gave an upper bound of the shape $\exp(-k/\log k)$, this would usually be considered extremely close to the optimal bound, but in this case would be insufficient to conclude (even heuristically) that there are only finitely many counterexamples.
